name: The Flickering Tomb

stars.name: The Pulse
stars.notes: Millisecond pulsar spinning 642 times per second. Electromagnetic emissions create a persistent strobe effect visible to the naked eye from nearby planets.

stars.name: The Cinder
stars.notes: Cooling white dwarf in a 12 AU orbit around the pulsar. Formerly a red giant whose outer layers were stripped by the pulsar's progenitor supernova.

planets.name: Stroboscope
planets.notes: Close pulsar orbit. The surface is bathed in 642-per-second radiation pulses, creating a visible strobe effect that makes the landscape appear to flicker. No atmosphere survives.

planets.name: The Cairn
planets.notes: Orbits the white dwarf. Heavily cratered surface suggests it predates the supernova event. Ancient—possibly older than either current star in its present form.

anomalies.name: Stroboscopic Illumination
anomalies.notes: The pulsar's 642 Hz rotation creates a radiation strobe that makes everything within 2 AU appear to flicker. Camera systems require specialized filtering. Human perception struggles—surfaces seem to jitter between illumination states.

anomalies.name: Pulsar Wind Nebula
anomalies.location: Expanding outward from The Pulse, concentrated in equatorial plane
anomalies.notes: Relativistic particle wind from the pulsar interacts with the white dwarf's remnant atmosphere, producing a faint nebular glow visible in X-ray and ultraviolet wavelengths.

anomalies.name: Temporal Interference Bands
anomalies.location: Between The Pulse and The Cinder
anomalies.notes: The combined gravitational fields of two stellar remnants create overlapping time dilation gradients. Precision clocks in the interstellar space between them show measurable temporal variance depending on exact position.

asteroid_belts.name: The Ossuary Belt
asteroid_belts.notes: Debris from the system's original planetary complement, shattered during the supernova that created The Pulse. Every fragment is intensely irradiated and structurally weakened.

stations.name: Flicker Station
stations.location: 15 AU from The Pulse, above orbital plane
stations.notes: Pulsar timing and white dwarf cooling-rate observatory. The station's most critical system is its radiation shielding; the second most critical is its flicker-compensating lighting.

faction_control.notes: Unclaimed. The system offers no habitable real estate, no extractable resources worth the radiation exposure, and a deeply unsettling perceptual environment.

history: The binary stellar remnant was cataloged in 2467 by an automated X-ray survey. The pairing of a millisecond pulsar with a white dwarf companion was noted as scientifically significant but not unique.

What made the system notable was the discovery of Stroboscope in 2489—a planet close enough to the pulsar for its radiation strobe to be visible on the surface. Early probe footage of the flickering landscape was widely circulated and gave the system its name.

Flicker Station was established in 2521 for pulsar timing research. Crew psychological reports consistently note discomfort related to the perceptual effects of the strobe, even with compensating lighting. Rotation periods were shortened to 60 days as a result.
description: The Flickering Tomb is a graveyard of stars lit by a strobe light. The Pulse—a millisecond pulsar spinning 642 times every second—shares the system with The Cinder, a cooling white dwarf, two irradiated planets, and a belt of shattered debris. The pulsar's radiation sweeps the inner system like a lighthouse beam accelerated to an insane frequency, and on the surface of Stroboscope, the closest planet, this creates a visible flicker: the landscape appears to judder between light and darkness hundreds of times per second. Instruments struggle. Human perception fails. The effect is profoundly disorienting.

The system's two stellar remnants are what remain of a binary that died in sequence. The more massive star went supernova first, creating The Pulse and stripping the companion down to its white dwarf core. The Cairn, orbiting The Cinder, may predate both deaths—a survivor from the system's original planetary complement, battered but enduring. The Ossuary Belt between them is wreckage, every fragment irradiated and slowly being ground to dust by the pulsar wind. Temporal interference bands in the space between the two remnants add gravitational complexity: clocks drift depending on position, and navigation requires constant correction.

No one lives here voluntarily for long. Flicker Station's 160 researchers endure 60-day rotations, the maximum before the perceptual effects of proximity to the strobe become psychologically debilitating even with compensating systems. The science is valuable—millisecond pulsar timing contributes to gravitational wave detection networks—but the experience is uniformly described as oppressive. The Flickering Tomb is a place where two stars died and left behind a system that cannot stop reminding you of the fact, 642 times per second.
